Avez-vous entendu dire si les landes de l'est sont tranquilles cette saison ?

J'élevais et dressais des chevaux sur les landes à l'est de la Montagne Solitaire, où l'herbe est maigre et les chevaux endurants. Je montais avant de savoir marcher correctement, et la moitié des montures de la vallée porte mon dressage.

Des pillards du Rhûn vinrent à la moisson et emmenèrent notre troupeau et la moitié de notre village. J'ai chevauché jusqu'à Val pour obtenir de l'aide, mais le conseil ne voulut pas m'entendre avant le matin ; alors j'ai rassemblé les valets de ferme et je les ai poursuivis moi-même.

Nous avons repris la plupart des chevaux et tous les enfants, mais deux valets de ferme ne sont pas revenus, et le village n'est plus qu'un cercle de poteaux calcinés. J'ai vendu le troupeau pour payer les familles des morts. Mes mains de cavalier sont tout ce qu'il me reste.
Tu as donné tout ce que tu avais. Cela compte.
Une tête brûlée qui part sans permission fait tuer des hommes.
Je chevaucherai pour vous avec joie, et je donnerai ma dernière pièce à quiconque vous voudrez aider.
Les éleveurs de chevaux des hautes landes de l'est élèvent des montures robustes et des cavaliers qui demandent peu. Nous sommes prompts à nous mettre en selle quand viennent les pillards.
Les murs tombent devant celui qui sait où ils sont faibles. Moi, je le sais.

J'ai dressé des tours de siège et des béliers pour un chef de guerre des hautes plaines, taillant un bois que nous, les Variags, n'avions jamais songé à employer. Quand l'armée du chef marcha sur une forteresse frontalière haradrim, mes engins l'accompagnèrent, et ses murs tremblèrent sous eux.

Après le siège, il me paya en captifs dont je n'avais que faire et en un cheval boiteux. Alors j'ai vendu les plans et deux béliers de rechange à un clan rival, et le chef a mis ma tête à prix ; ses cavaliers me pourchassent encore.

Je possède un maillet, une mauvaise réputation et la carte de tous les gués entre ici et les Monts Cendrés. Les morts de ces enclos n'ont jamais troublé mon sommeil, mais la dette d'un salaire impayé, si.
Un homme capable de briser les murs vaut plus qu'un homme qui se contente de les escalader.
Tu as trompé ton propre chef. Pourquoi serais-je à l'abri de toi ?
Donnez-moi du bois et quelques bras, et je vous bâtirai de quoi ouvrir n'importe quelle porte.
Je suis un bâtisseur de machines de siège issu des clans variags, et je vais là où les murs sont épais et la solde plus épaisse encore.
J'ai juré ma lame une fois. Je la jurerais encore, si l'homme en valait la peine.

J'étais frère de lame juré de l'héritier d'un clan de cavaliers, et nous avons chevauché ensemble depuis l'enfance. J'ai gagné ma place dans la bande de guerre à l'épée, contre des hommes plus âgés, et je n'ai jamais perdu un duel qu'on m'ait donné.

L'héritier ordonna de passer à la hache un garde de caravane qui s'était rendu, et je me suis interposé. Il m'a frappé au visage, et son clan m'a nommé briseur de serment, ce qui, au Khand, est pire que d'être nommé mort.
Je porte mon épée, ma cicatrice et la honte d'un serment qui me liait à un boucher. Je n'ai ni clan, ni camp, et plus personne pour partager un feu avec moi.
Garder foi envers les sans-défense n'est pas une honte. La honte était la sienne.
Un serment est un serment. Tu as rompu le tien, quelles qu'en soient les raisons.
Nommez-moi une cause que je puisse servir sans abaisser mon épée, et je vous suivrai jusqu'au bout.
Je suis un épéiste variag qui servait la maisonnée d'un chef de clan, et je combats le mieux en tête d'une charge.
J'observe ce pays depuis trente ans. Demandez-moi n'importe quoi sur les plaines et je vous dirai qui les traverse à cheval.

J'étais archer à cheval et éclaireur pour les caravanes qui traversent les plaines du Khand vers les routes du sud. Je connaissais chaque puits, chaque creux propice aux embuscades, et quels pillards haradrim acceptaient de l'or pour regarder ailleurs.

Une saison, le chef qui m'avait engagé vendit notre route aux pillards mêmes contre lesquels nous veillions. J'ai averti les maîtres de caravane et abattu deux de ses hommes pour cela, et il m'a congédié avant la venue des pluies.
Maintenant je chevauche seul, avec un arc, un bon œil et un nom que les maîtres de caravane prononcent à voix basse. Les gardes honnêtes sont rares, et les chefs qui les paient plus rares encore.
Un homme qui tient parole envers ceux qui l'engagent vaut plus que l'or de n'importe quel chef.
Tu as tué des hommes de ton propre camp. N'attends pas que je t'en félicite.
S'il vous faut des yeux en avant de votre colonne et une flèche qui trouve sa cible, j'éclairerai la route pour vous.
Je suis un éclaireur des plaines et un archer à cheval qui a parcouru les routes de caravane entre le Khand et les marchés du sud.
Approchez, je ne mords pas. Sauf si la plaie suppure déjà.

J'ai appris le métier du couteau enfant, dans un camp de guerre variag, tenant les lampes pendant que le chirurgien recousait des hommes qui avaient perdu leurs paris contre une hache. À vingt ans, je savais remettre un os, brûler une gangrène et maudire une fièvre plus vite que quiconque au sud des Monts Cendrés.

J'ai distribué le vin de blessure et les bandages du chef à quiconque en demandait, même à un éclaireur haradrim captif, et le chef m'a passé la lanière sur le dos pour avoir gaspillé ses réserves sur l'ennemi. Je ne suis pas resté pour voir ce qu'il préparait ensuite.
Je porte encore une trousse d'aiguilles, une bouteille d'alcool et une conscience dont nul ne m'avait prévenu. Je continue de rapiécer les gens et je me demande encore pourquoi cela ne paie jamais.
Tu as réparé ce que les chefs brisent. Cela vaut bien plus que les réserves dépensées.
Des soins gratuits pour l'ennemi, c'est juste une manière élégante de l'armer.
Je recoudrai vos blessés et vos ennemis aussi, si vous supportez d'y assister.
Je suis un chirurgien de camp des armées variags, recousant les coups de hache et les entailles de flèche pour quiconque a de l'or ou de la bonté.
Chaque route a son prix. Je connais le prix de la plupart.

J'étais agent des caravanes d'esclaves qui descendaient des marchés du Khand vers la côte du Harad. Je tenais les registres, soudoyais les péagers, et j'ai acheté et vendu plus d'hommes et de chevaux que je ne saurais compter.

Un associé en qui j'avais confiance vendit tout le convoi à des acheteurs orientaux pendant mon sommeil, et je suis resté dans la poussière avec les registres et une bourse vide. La cargaison, je ne l'ai pas pleurée, mais l'argent, si.
Je ne possède rien, sinon une tête faite pour les comptes et une longue liste d'hommes qui me doivent de l'argent. J'ai l'intention de me faire payer par chacun d'eux avant de mourir.
Un homme capable de tirer profit de rien est utile à n'importe quelle cause.
Tu as vendu des hommes. Je ne l'oublierai pas, aussi poli sois-tu.
Confiez-moi vos fonds et vos caravanes, et vous verrez des bénéfices avant la fin de la saison.
Je suis un courtier de caravanes venu des marchés du Khand, et je sais comment l'argent circule entre les plaines et le sud.
Vous avez l'air de quelqu'un qui possède quelque chose qui vaut la peine d'être pris. Rassurez-vous, je ne fais qu'admirer.
J'ai grandi à l'ombre d'un camp de guerre, à faire les poches des guerriers et à receler leur butin. Adulte, je pouvais vider la tente d'un chef sans réveiller les chiens.

J'ai volé le trésor de guerre d'un clan, et quand les cavaliers m'ont encerclé, j'ai livré les noms de toute ma bande pour sauver ma peau. Je ne prétends pas que ce fût courageux, seulement que cela a marché.
J'ai quelques pièces, une lame affûtée et un talent pour me tirer d'affaire dont je ne devrais pas être fier. Je le suis pourtant, et les clans n'oublient jamais un visage.
Un voleur habile sait quand fuir. Tu as survécu pour le raconter.
Tu as trahi les tiens. Je ferais mieux de vérifier ma bourse.
Prenez-moi avec vous, et je trouverai ce que vos ennemis cachent, en gardant mes mains pour moi, la plupart du temps.
Je suis voleur et receleur des camps de guerre variags, et je connais tous les passages dérobés menant à la tente d'un chef.
J'ai commandé quarante cavaliers à dix-neuf ans. J'en aurais commandé quatre cents, si on m'en avait donné l'occasion.

J'ai pris le commandement d'une bande de guerre des plaines quand son capitaine est tombé à un gué, et j'ai gagné mon premier combat par une feinte qui a attiré une colonne haradrim dans un ravin. L'été suivant, les cavaliers me donnaient un titre que je n'avais pas encore mérité.

J'ai gardé le butin pour moi et payé mes hommes en promesses, et les promesses se sont épuisées avant l'hiver. La moitié a déserté au camp suivant, et les autres m'ont suivi comme des spectres jusqu'à ce que je les libère.
J'ai une épée, un bon cheval, et une leçon à moitié apprise sur ce qui pousse les hommes à suivre. Je n'ai pas l'intention de perdre un second commandement.
Un chef apprend plus d'une défaite que de dix victoires.
Tu as floué des hommes qui ont saigné pour toi. Seul un sot commande ainsi.
Donnez-moi des cavaliers et un plan, et je vous montrerai ce qu'une feinte variag fait à une ligne de bataille.
Je suis un jeune capitaine de bande de guerre des cavaliers variags, formé à lire un champ de bataille et à briser une ligne.
Vous voulez une hache qui ne se brisera pas au premier coup ? Bien. Rares sont ceux qui savent le demander.

J'ai forgé des armes dans un camp du Khand pendant vingt ans, ces haches courbes et tranchantes dont mon peuple est renommé, équilibrées et avides. Chaque lame que je faisais, je l'éprouvais sur un billot de chêne de fer avant de la vendre.

Le chef m'a ordonné de forger des colliers et des chaînes pour ses caravanes d'esclaves, et j'ai refusé, bien qu'il m'offrît le double d'argent. Il a réduit ma forge en cendres, avec les outils que mon père m'avait laissés.
Je ne porte qu'un marteau, une main balafrée, et une fierté obstinée qui m'a tout coûté. Je ne l'ai jamais regretté, et je doute de le regretter un jour.
Un artisan qui refuse de forger des chaînes rend tout de même le monde meilleur.
Tu aurais pu forger ces colliers et vivre dans l'opulence. L'orgueil est un bien mauvais marché.
Fournissez-moi une forge et du fer, et j'armerai vos gens mieux qu'aucun forgeron du sud.
Je suis forgeron de haches des camps du Khand, et je sais faire une lame qui mord à travers heaume et os.
Il n'est aucune créature au monde que je comprenne mieux qu'un cheval. Les gens sont plus difficiles.

J'étais dresseur de chevaux et lancier dans un clan dont la richesse tenait à ses troupeaux. Je domptais les poulains sauvages des plaines, je chevauchais la crête à l'aube, et je chargeais en tête des lances quand le clan partait en guerre.

Lors d'un raid de vendetta, j'ai trouvé un garçon blessé du clan rival caché dans un ravin ; je l'ai hissé sur mon cheval et ramené aux tentes des siens. Mon clan a appelé cela trahison, et mon propre chef a fait emmener mon troupeau.
Il me reste un cheval, le poulain dont je n'ai pu me séparer, et une selle qui est encore mienne. Les plaines m'appellent toujours, mais aucun clan ne veut de moi.
Tu as fait preuve de pitié quand il ne te restait que cela. Ce n'est pas une trahison.
Tu as aidé l'enfant de l'ennemi. Ton clan avait raison d'être en colère.
Donnez-moi un cheval et une lance, et je porterai votre bannière en tête de chaque charge.
Je suis dresseur de chevaux et lancier des clans des plaines, élevé en selle parmi les troupeaux du Khand.
Je serai honnête avec vous. Je ne suis pas courageux, mais je suis très difficile à toucher.

J'ai été formé comme archer dans une ligne de bataille variag, tirant depuis l'arrière tandis que les haches tenaient le front. Je pouvais planter une flèche dans une gorge cuirassée à deux cents pas, et je tirais fierté du nombre de traits qui restaient dans mon carquois.

Quand la ligne a cédé lors d'une guerre de frontière contre les Haradrim, j'ai tiré jusqu'à ce que les cors sonnent, puis j'ai lâché mon arc et j'ai couru. Mieux vaut vivre en lâche que mourir en cadavre, me suis-je dit, et je me le répète chaque nuit depuis.
Je suis déserteur désormais, avec une prime sur ma tête dans les camps de guerre et un arc acéré dont je n'ai jamais su cesser de me servir. La peur m'a rendu prudent, et je suis encore en vie.
Fuir un combat perdu n'est pas de la lâcheté. Tu as gardé ton bras.
Tu as laissé tes camarades mourir. Je ne me fie pas à ce genre de cran.
Garde-moi derrière ta ligne avec un arc et une cible dégagée, et je vaudrai chaque pièce.
Je suis un archer des lignes de bataille variags, entraîné à tirer derrière les haches et à rester en vie.
Every cask on the quay at Tharbad has a number, and I knew them all...

I kept the stores and the river wharves at Tharbad for the lord warden, who trusted my tally over his own eyes. I knew which bridge piers would stand the spring flood and to the week how long the grain would last. The merchants did not enjoy my company.

The winter Dunlending bands crossed the Greyflood ice, farm folk crowded the quay begging passage into the town, and we had bread for half of them. I advised that the river gate stay barred, and it did. The garrison ate until spring, and the warden never spoke to me again.

I do not regret the sum, only that it fell to me. His kin found me a clerkship in a village with no granary, which is to say no post at all. Now I sell my reckoning to anyone sensible enough to buy it.
Someone must do the sum, and you did it honestly.
You barred the gate on your own people and called it arithmetic.
Hand me a company to feed and a ford to hold, and I will make the stores last.
The quartermasters of Tharbad keep the wharves and the granaries, and we answer for every hard sum the river gate demands. Merchants seldom thank us for it.
If you came to tell me I was wrong at Sarn Ford, save your breath. I have heard it all...

I was a spearman of the Sarn Ford garrison, first into the water in every drill and first to volunteer for every sortie. My sergeant called me the best arm in the company and the worst ear. I took both as praise.

When a goblin band broke and ran for the hills, I led the chase against orders. We ran down every one, even those who threw away their blades, but two of my own fell in a gully I never scouted. The sergeant took my spear in front of the whole ford.
I do not grieve for the goblins, only for the two who followed me. Since then I walk alone, and a spear needs a line behind it. I would have it be a line worth following.
Courage that outruns orders can still be steered.
Two good men died because you wanted a chase.
Set me at the front and tell me when to stop, and I will stop.
The spearmen of Sarn Ford are first into the water and last to hear an order. Most of us have paid for it at least once.
Mind my pack, stranger. I have carried it a long way and mean to carry it further...

I grew up in the reed marshes of Swanfleet, where my father hunted wildfowl and my mother salted eels for the barge traders. By fifteen I could put an arrow through a heron in flight. We ate what the marsh gave, and some winters it gave little.

The year the floods came early, a troop of horsemen rode through asking for food in the king's name. My father gave them half our store, and by midwinter my brother was dead of hunger. Nobody from the capital ever came back to repay it.

I took the bow upriver the next spring and have kept every coin since. I fight well and I am not afraid, but I give nothing away, because I learned what giving costs. Pay me fairly and I will never leave my post.
You have earned your caution, and your bow.
Then you carry a grudge and call it thrift.
I can put arrows where you need them, if the pay is steady and honest.
Marsh folk of Swanfleet live on wildfowl, eels and whatever the tide leaves. We learn early to count every arrow and every coin.
Patrol routes, ford depths, watch rotas. I know them all. Few have asked what they are worth...

I commanded a patrol company out of Tharbad, twelve years a captain on the Greenway south of the Barrow-downs. I knew every track from the Greyflood to the Brandywine. The men respected me and I let them.

A barge smuggler offered coin for the hours my patrols passed each crossing. I took it, then took more; the road was long and a captain's pay was short. A rival officer counted the gaps and carried them to the lord warden.
I left before the hearing, with my purse and my maps. Call me a traitor if you like. I sold a schedule, not a gate, and I still know every road in Minhiriath.
A short purse tempts many officers; the ones who stop are rarer.
You sold the road to smugglers. Next it will be orcs.
I can plan your march and your ambushes. My price is plain, and I name it first.
The patrol captains of Tharbad walk the Greenway and the river tracks, and we know every ford and landing. Some of us sell that knowledge more freely than we should.
I would rather you did not ask which company I came from...
I was a young pikeman levied from a farm near Andrath, one of three hundred sent to hold the line below the old barrows. I drilled hard and bragged of it. In truth I had never seen blood.

When a Gundabad warband hit our shield wall at dawn, I felt the ranks tremble and ran. I left the man beside me, a friend from home, still holding his place. I heard later the line held another hour and he did not come back.
I sold my pike in Tharbad for bread and slept in barges for a season. Deserters are called traitors, and perhaps I am one. Still, I am alive, and I would take pay for another chance.
Fear has killed more good men than any warband.
You left a friend to die and now you want wages?
I will stand, if the pay is good and the line behind me is thick.
Levies from the farms around Andrath are sent to hold the line below the old barrows. Not all of us stand when the warbands come.
I lost a company once. Forty spears, and I buried none of them...
I led forty men on the Greenway, sworn to the king and to each other. We held the road from Sarn Ford down to Tharbad for three summers. Every man of mine could be trusted at my back.

Dunlending raiders burned a farm at Girdley that belonged to my wife's kin and left nothing standing. I pulled my company off the road to hunt them and found them camped. We killed them all, wounded and captive alike, and I did not stop my hand.
The lord warden called it butchery and broke the company. Half my men went home; the rest followed other captains. I am not sorry, only alone.
Grief has bent harder men than you.
You threw away forty men to feed a grudge.
Give me forty spears and a road, and I will hold it to the last.
The Greenway companies hold the road from Sarn Ford to Tharbad for the king. We are sworn to each other, and the Dunlending raiders have given many of us cause for hatred.
You are bleeding on the road. I know a wound when I see one, and a lost cause too...
At fourteen I was taken in by a healer who kept the infirmary at Minas Eithel. She taught me to sew a wound and set a bone, and to bear what cannot be cured. I worked her ward through three winters.

After a fight at the river ford, thirty wounded came in at once and we had herbs for ten. I treated those who could fight again and let the rest go as gently as I could manage. She called it murder and said she would not train a hand that chose.
I left that night. Since then I have stitched men across Cardolan, by roadside fires and in drovers' camps. I am not gentle, but my patients walk away more often than not.
Someone must choose, and you saved the ones you could.
A healer who abandons the dying is no healer.
Take me on and your wounded will walk again, the ones who can.
Healers of Minas Eithel work the old infirmary and the riverbank, where the wounded outnumber the herbs. We learn to choose, and not everyone forgives that.
A hero of the Tharbad road, at your service, or so the dispatches said...

I am the second son of a Dúnedain house whose lands lie mostly in my grandfather's memory. My elder brother had the title, and I had a sword and a talent for being noticed. In Caras Gorthad I commanded a company of sixty, which sounds finer than it was.

After a brush with some goblin scouts I wrote to the king that I had routed a host. I had routed four goblins and a donkey, but the letter was well written. The king granted me a manor on the strength of it, until a rider passed through and asked where the bodies were.
I lost the manor before I had seen it. Since then I have lived by wit, which is thin fare in a land of horsemen and spears. I did kill the four goblins, though. Nobody ever mentions that.
Four goblins is still four fewer than before.
You lied to the king and are surprised it caught up with you.
Take me on, and I swear to report only what happened. Mostly.
Second sons of the Dúnedain houses of Cardolan inherit a sword and not much else. Some of us write our own legends to make up the difference.
I have walked the Barrow-downs since I could walk. Do not ask me to be gentle there...

I was a ranger of Tyrn Gorthad, trained by an old captain who taught me to move unseen and leave no track. For six years I watched the road below the barrows and counted every Dunlending band that passed. I was the best scout on the downs, and I knew it.

When a Dunlending envoy came under a white cloth to speak with the captain, I shot him from the barrow-top before he said a word. I judged that anything from that country carried a lie. The captain disowned me before the other rangers, for breaking a truce was not our way.
I took my bow and went south. The rangers say I broke faith. His escort carried pitch and torches meant for the villages below, and nobody thanks me for that.
If the torches were real, you saved those villages.
A truce broken once is never trusted again.
Use me as your eyes and your bow. I will see them coming, and I will not wait for a white cloth.
Rangers of Tyrn Gorthad watch the road below the barrows and count every Dunlending band. We are hard folk, and not every captain approves of our methods.
Honest work is for those who can afford it. Care to hear about the other kind...

I ran a toll on the river road with a dozen hard men, and for a long while it was almost legal. We took a share of every grain wagon bound for Tharbad and called it protection. The wagons were never robbed while we were paid, which is more than the king's patrols could say.

Then grain ran short at Caras Gorthad, and the garrison went hungry while my men sat on stored sacks. A clerk worked out where it had gone. My company scattered at the first sound of the king's riders, and I, the leader, scattered fastest.
I keep a lighter purse now, and no company at all. So here I stand, an honest wanderer at last, for want of better offers. I will admit the grain was not my best work.
A thief can learn what hunger costs, same as anyone.
You starved a garrison to fatten your purse.
Hire me. I know every thief on the river road, which makes me oddly useful against them.
Traders and toll-keepers on the river road live off the grain wagons bound for Tharbad. A few of us take a larger share than the king allows.
I made a promise at Downsend once, and I have not yet found a way to keep it...

I was a ranger who served as warden of Downsend, guarding it against wolves and Dunlending raiders. The villagers fed me, mended my cloak and made me one of their own. I swore on the boundary stone that I would not let their roofs burn.

My captain called every ranger to the Barrow-downs to meet a Gundabad column. Duty bound me, so I went, and in nine days the column was beaten. When I returned Downsend was ash, and a dozen of its children were gone, taken or dead; no one could say which.
I kept my oath to the king and broke my word to them, and I cannot tell which weighs more. I have searched the old roads for the taken ever since. I will not stop until I know what became of them.
No one can stand in two places. You did what duty asked.
You swore to guard them, then walked away. Oaths come cheap.
Let me search beside you, and I will give my bow and my word to your road.
The rangers who ward the villages of Cardolan swear to keep their roofs from burning. Duty calls us away as often as it keeps us home.
Forgive me. Have you any bread to spare? Not for me, you understand...

I was a house guard in the hall of a minor lord near Barrowfield. He paid little and I gave most of it away, to the widows of the garrison and the families of horsemen who did not come back. A guard's work is quiet, and I liked that mine was useful.

A goblin raid burned the hall one winter night. The lord died on the stair and I carried his reeve's children out. The survivors of the village, nearly forty, followed me to Caras Gorthad, where the king's officers found them a corner of a warehouse and little else.
I stay with them when I can and send what I earn, which is never enough. A guard with no hall is a guard for hire, and I will take any honest wage that feeds them.
Keeping those people alive is worth more than any battle.
One sword and no wage will not feed forty mouths.
Pay a fair wage and spare a ration for my people, and my sword is yours.
Guards in the halls of the minor lords near Barrowfield earn little and keep the village widows fed. When a hall burns, the survivors turn to us.
Have you a moment? The families at the river gate need someone to speak for them...

I was a junior clerk to the king's treasurers at Caras Gorthad, tallying grain and writing letters for lords who could not write their own. I was good with people, and the old clerks sent me to talk to the angry ones. I came to like it.

When families fleeing the burned farms along the Greyflood reached the capital by the hundreds, a lord argued the gates should close to save the stores. I wrote down their names, kept a ledger of who was sick and who was starving, and put it before the council. They called it sentiment and had me removed from my post.

I learned that a ledger can be a plea if you write it well. Now I go from town to town gathering food, coin and sworn blades for those families. Cardolan is not rich, but there is more kindness in it than anyone admits.
A list of names can save lives, and you made one.
The council was right to count the stores before it counted feelings.
Take me along, and I will find you food, goodwill and honest allies.
The king's treasurers at Caras Gorthad keep the counts of grain and refugees. A few of us have spoken up for the border farmers and been sent away for it.
The tower at Cameth Brin stands because someone counted every stone and every mouth...

I kept the stores and the wall-works at Cameth Brin, under a castellan who trusted my tally over his own eyes. I knew which stretches of wall would hold and which would crack, and to the day how long the grain would last. Few in the tower liked how I spoke of it.

The autumn the trolls came down from the Ettenmoors, hill families crowded the gate begging shelter we could not feed. I advised that the gate stay shut, and it did. The garrison lived through the winter, and the castellan never looked at me again.

I do not regret the sum, only that it fell to me to make it. His friends found me a post at a far outpost with no walls, which is to say none. Now I sell my reckoning to anyone with the sense to use it.
Hard choices fall on whoever sees clearly enough to make them.
You shut out hill families and called it arithmetic.
Give me a company to feed and a tower to hold, and I will make the numbers work.
The quartermasters of Cameth Brin keep the grain and the wall-works, and we answer for every hard sum the tower demands. Few in the town thank us for it.
If you came to tell me I was wrong at the Hoarwell, save your breath. I have heard it...

I was a spearman of the Egladil watch in the Angle, first over the ditch in every drill and first to volunteer for every sortie. My captain called me the best arm in the company and the worst ear. I took both as praise.

When an orc band broke and fled along the river, I led the chase against orders. We ran down every one, even those who threw down their blades, but two of my own fell in a bog I never scouted. The captain stripped me of my place before the whole watch.
I mourn no orcs, only the two who followed me. I walk alone now, and a spear is wasted without a line at its back. Let it be a line worth the trouble.
A fierce spear is still a spear. It only needs a hand to steer it.
Two men are dead because you wanted the chase.
Put me at the front, give me a signal to halt, and I will heed it.
The spearmen of the Egladil watch are first over the ditch and last to hear an order. Most of us have been punished for it at least once.
Mind my pack, stranger. I have carried it a long way and I mean to carry it further...

I grew up on the Coldfells, where my father hunted mountain hare and my mother spun fleece for the peddlers who climbed up from the valleys. By fifteen I could put an arrow through a raven on the wing. We lived on what the hunt gave, and some winters it gave little.

The year the snow came early, a patrol of the lords' men passed through asking for food in the king's name. My father gave them half our store, and by midwinter my brother was dead of hunger. Nobody from Cameth Brin ever came to repay it.

I took my bow down the valley the next spring and have kept every coin since. I fight well and I am not afraid, but I give nothing away, because I learned what giving costs. Pay me fairly and I will never leave my post.
Your caution was bought dearly, and so was your bow.
So you nurse a grudge and call it thrift.
I can put arrows where you need them, if the pay is steady and honest.
Hill folk of the Coldfells live on game, fleece and whatever the season gives. We learn early to count every arrow and every coin.
Patrol routes, ford depths, watch rotas. I know them all. Few have asked what they are worth...
I commanded a patrol company at Last Bridge, twelve years a captain on the East Road. I knew every track from the Ettenmoors to the Loudwater. The men respected me and I let them.

A caravan master offered coin for the hours my patrols passed each crossing. I took it, then took more; the road was long and a captain's pay was short. A rival officer counted the gaps and carried them to the commander of the bridge.
I left before the hearing, with my purse and my maps. Call me a traitor if you like. I sold a timetable, not a gate, and I still know every road between the rivers.
A thin purse tempts many captains; the ones who stop are rarer.
Today you sell the road to caravans. Tomorrow it will be trolls.
I can plan your marches and your ambushes. My price is plain, and I name it first.
The patrol captains of Last Bridge walk the East Road and the Hoarwell crossings, and we know every ford and track. Some of us sell that knowledge more freely than we should.
I would rather you did not ask which company I came from...
I was a young pikeman levied from a hill farm in Ettendale, one of three hundred sent to hold the line below the hold. I drilled hard and bragged of it. In truth I had never seen blood.

When a Gundabad warband struck our shield wall at first light, I felt the ranks shake and I ran. I left the man beside me, a boy from my own valley, still holding his place. I heard later the line stood another hour and he never came home.
I sold my pike at Last Bridge for bread and slept in sheepfolds for a season. Deserters are called traitors, and perhaps I am one. Still, I am alive, and I would take pay for another chance.
Terror finishes more men than steel does.
You ran from a friend and now you want coin?
I can fight, if the pay is good and there are enough shields beside me.
Levies from the hill farms of Ettendale are sent to hold the line below the hold. Not all of us stand when the warbands come.
I lost a company once. Forty swords, and I buried none of them...
I led forty men on the East Road, sworn to the king and to each other. We held the road between Last Bridge and the Trollshaws for three summers. Every man of mine could be trusted at my back.

Gundabad raiders burned a steading in the Angle that belonged to my wife's kin and left nothing standing. I pulled my company off the road to hunt them and found them camped. We killed them all, wounded and captive alike, and I did not stop my hand.
The lord of Egladil called it butchery and broke the company. Half my men went home; the rest followed other captains. I am not sorry, only alone.
Grief has bent many a good captain.
You broke your company to feed your own revenge.
Give me forty sound men and a road, and I will hold it past the last of us.
The East Road companies hold the way between Last Bridge and the Trollshaws for the king. We are sworn to each other, and the Gundabad raiders have given many of us cause for hatred.
You are bleeding on the road. I know a wound when I see one, and a lost cause too...
At fourteen I was taken in by a healer who kept the infirmary at Egladil. She taught me to sew a wound and set a bone, and to bear what cannot be cured. I worked her ward through three winters.

After a skirmish where the two rivers meet, thirty wounded came in at once and we had herbs for ten. I tended the ones who could fight again and let the rest slip away as easily as I could manage. She called it murder and said she would not train a hand that chose.
I left that night. Since then I have stitched men across the hills, by roadside fires and in shepherds' huts. I am not gentle, but my patients walk away more often than not.
Somebody had to choose, and you chose to save the fighters.
A healer who walks away from the dying has forgotten the trade.
Bring me along and your wounded will walk again, those who can.
Healers of Egladil work the old infirmary at the meeting of the rivers, where the wounded outnumber the herbs. We learn to choose, and not everyone forgives that.
A hero of the Trollshaws, at your service, or so the dispatches said...

I am the second son of a Dúnedain house whose lands lie mostly in my grandfather's memory. My elder brother held the title, and I held a sword and a gift for being noticed. At Egladil I commanded a company of sixty, which sounds finer than it was.

After a brush with some goblin scouts I sent word to the king that I had routed a host. I had routed four goblins and a lame mule, but the dispatch was well written. The king granted me a hill farm on the strength of it, until a ranger passed through and asked where the bodies were.
I was stripped of the farm before I had seen it. Since then I have lived by wit, which is thin fare in hill country. I did kill the four goblins, though. Nobody ever mentions that.
Four goblins less is four goblins less.
You lied to the king and are shocked he found out.
Hire me, and I will report only what truly happened. Mostly.
Younger sons of the Dúnedain lords of the Angle grow up with a sword and no land. Some of us write our own legends to make up for it.
I have walked the Ettenmoors since I could walk. Do not ask me to be gentle there...

I was a ranger of the Trollshaws, trained by an old captain who taught me to move unseen and leave no track. For six years I watched the road below the fells and counted every orc that passed. I was the best scout in the hills, and I knew it.

When a Gundabad envoy came under a white cloth to speak with the captain, I shot him from the rocks before he said a word. I judged that anything from that country carried a lie. The captain disowned me before the other rangers, for breaking a truce was not our way.
I took my bow and left the Shaws. The rangers say I broke faith. His escort carried pitch and torches meant for the hill villages, and nobody thanks me for that.
If the torches were real, you saved those villages.
No one trusts a truce that has been broken once.
Make me your eyes and your bow. I will see them coming, and I will not wait for a white cloth.
Rangers of the Trollshaws watch the fells and count every orc band that passes. We are hard folk, and not every captain approves of our methods.
Honest work is for those who can afford it. Care to hear about the other kind...

I ran a toll at Last Bridge with a dozen hard men, and for a long while it was almost legal. We took a share of every grain wagon bound for Cameth Brin and called it protection. The wagons were never robbed while we were paid, which is more than the king's patrols could say.

Then grain ran short in the tower, and the garrison went hungry while my men sat on stored sacks. A bookkeeper worked out where it had gone. My company scattered at the first sound of the king's riders, and I, the leader, scattered fastest.
My purse is lighter now, and my company is gone entirely. I am an honest wanderer at last, though only for lack of offers. The grain, I admit, was not my finest work.
Hunger teaches even a thief something.
You starved the tower to line your pockets.
Hire me. I know every thief on the East Road, which makes me oddly useful against them.
Traders and toll-keepers at Last Bridge live off the grain wagons bound for Cameth Brin. A few of us take a larger share than the king allows.
I made a promise in Ettendale once, and I have not yet found a way to keep it...

I was a ranger who served as warden of a hamlet in Ettendale, guarding it against wolves and hill trolls. The villagers fed me, mended my cloak and made me one of their own. I swore on the gatepost that I would not let their roofs burn.

My captain called every ranger to the Ettenmoors to meet a troll pack and its orc drovers. Duty bound me, so I went, and in nine days the pack was broken. When I returned the hamlet was ash, and a dozen of its children were gone, taken or dead; no one could say which.

I kept my oath to the king and broke my word to them, and I cannot say which weighs more. I have searched the old trails for the taken ever since, and I will not stop until I know what became of them.
Duty pulled you away. That is not the same as abandoning them.
You swore to guard them and left anyway. Your word was thin.
Let me search with you, and my bow and my word are yours on the road.
The rangers who ward the hamlets of Ettendale swear to keep their roofs from burning. Duty calls us away as often as it keeps us home.
Forgive me. Have you any bread to spare? Not for me, you understand...

I was a house guard in the hall of a minor lord on the edge of the Coldfells. He paid little and I gave most of it away, to the widows of the garrison and the families of shepherds who did not come back. A guard's work is quiet, and I liked that mine was useful.

A troll raid broke the hall one winter night and set it ablaze. The lord died on the stair and I carried his reeve's children out. The survivors of the village, nearly forty, followed me to Cameth Brin, where the king's officers found them a corner of a granary and little else.
I visit when I can and send what I earn, which is never enough. A guard without a hall is a sword for hire, and any honest wage that feeds them will do.
Feeding the survivors is as good a fight as any.
One sword and no pay cannot feed forty.
Pay a fair wage, spare a ration for my people, and I will serve you faithfully.
Guards in the halls of the minor lords on the Coldfells earn little and keep the village widows fed. When a hall burns, the survivors turn to us.
Have you a moment? The families at the tower gate need someone to speak for them...

I was a junior clerk to the king's treasurers at Cameth Brin, tallying grain and writing letters for hill chiefs who could not write their own. I was good with people, and the old clerks sent me to talk to the angry ones. I came to like it.

When families fleeing the burned hill villages reached the tower town by the hundreds, a lord argued the gates should close to save the stores. I wrote down their names, kept a ledger of who was sick and who was starving, and laid it before the council. They called it sentiment and had me removed from my post.

I learned that a ledger can be a plea if you write it well. Now I go from hold to hold gathering food, coin and sworn blades for those families. Rhudaur is poor, but there is more kindness in it than anyone admits.
Those names on your ledger are alive because you wrote them down.
The council counted the stores first, and rightly.
Bring me along, and I will find you provisions, goodwill and honest allies.
The king's treasurers at Cameth Brin keep the counts of grain and refugees. A few of us have spoken up for the hill families and been sent away for it.
A cave-in sorts the living from the dead faster than any healer. I learned to keep pace with it...

I was bone-setter to the iron mines under Belegost. When a gallery came down I went in after it with splints, poppy and a lamp, and I learned to judge in a breath who would mend and who would not. Between falls I drew the shoring plans myself, since the hewers kept building them wrong.

The winter the east gallery fell, a Broadbeam lord's son was carried out beside a dozen hewers. His wound would have taken all my poppy and all my night, and he would still have died. I tended the hewers. Every one of them walked out of that mine, and his father has not forgiven me.

The Broadbeams closed the hospice doors to me, and no house in the Blue Mountains will cross them for a bone-setter. So I walk the Dwarf-road with my satchel and sell what I know to whoever has wounded to mend.
You saved twelve lives with a choice no one else would make.
A lord's son left to die by his own healer. I would not forgive it either.
I will mend your wounded and shore up your siege works, and I will not waste either on a lost cause.
I was a bone-setter in the mines of Belegost until I let a lord's son die to save his hewers. Now I mend whoever pays.
Goblins never stay dead in the Blue Mountains. There are always more of them in the north...

I held the shield-wall at Dwarrowgate for nine winters against the Blue Craig raiders, and I trained the young hewers there in axe-work and in how to keep their feet when the line pushes. We gave the goblins no quarter. They learned to come at night.

One night they took a wagon of ore and two carters on the Dwarf-road. I led my company after them into the Craig, through tunnels no dwarf had mapped, against the warden's order. We brought the carters back. We left four of our own in those tunnels, and the warden broke my rank at the gate.

I would do it again, and the warden knows it, which is why he will not have me back. So I carry my axe where a fighting dwarf is still wanted. There is no shortage of goblins between here and the Misty Mountains.
You went after your own. Few captains would.
Four dead to bring back two. Your warden had a point.
Give me a shield-wall to stand in and I will hold it, whatever comes over it.
I fought the goblins of Blue Craig at Dwarrowgate until I broke an order to chase them home. I want a fight worth having.
In Nogrod a younger son inherits a name and nothing else...

My father is a lord of the Firebeards, and my elder brother will hold his hall after him. I was raised to command all the same: drill, siegecraft, the keeping of stores and accounts. My tutors said I had the makings of a captain. Nobody said what I was to be captain of.

When the warden of Hammerdeep died I asked for his command, and the council gave it to a cousin twice my age. I told them what I thought of him in front of the whole hall. My father said I could apologize or leave Nogrod until I had learned some manners.
I took my gear and my savings and nothing else. A dwarf can win a hall of his own out in the world, if he has the wit and the axe for it. I mean to come home with a name the council cannot pass over.
Ambition is no crime. A captain needs a company to prove himself.
You shamed your elders before the hall and call it ambition.
Give me a company to lead and I will show you what Nogrod passed over.
A younger son of the Firebeards, passed over for a command. I mean to win a name of my own.
Fight goblins long enough and you learn to smell the next raid coming...

I spent forty years on the northern marches, first on the walls of Stonewatch and then raising them. I know how the Blue Craig tribes think, when they move and where they strike. Every spring I told the council that the old north gate would not hold.

They would not pay for new stone, so I made them pay another way. When the goblins came that autumn I gave up the north gate without a fight and held the inner wall. Nobody died who need have, and the council voted the stone within the month. Then a sentry told them I had known the raid was coming.
They called it treachery. I call it the only argument the council ever listened to. Either way my command is gone, but I know my trade, and there is always work for a captain who wins.
Hard sense. You got your wall and lost no one for it.
You let goblins through your own gate to win an argument.
I will plan your battles and build your walls, and I will win them in my own way.
A captain of the northern marches who gave up a gate to win a quarrel with the council. Exiled, but I still win.
Every caravan on the Dwarf-road needs a guide, and every guide has his price...

I guided the iron caravans from Thorin's Halls along the Dwarf-road, through the Shire and on to Bree. I know every ford on the Brandywine, every inn that waters its beer and every hedge a hobbit thinks is his. The pay was poor for so much knowing.

So I sold some of it. A Bree-land gang paid well to learn which wagons carried ore and which carried silver, and when to expect them. It went smoothly for three seasons, until the Bree watch took the gang and the gang named its friends. My house struck my name from its rolls before the warden could send for me.
I have no house now and no name in the Blue Mountains, and no shame in what I know. The roads of Eriador are full of folk who will pay a guide who sees things as they are.
A guide who knows both sides of the road could be useful.
You sold your own kin's wagons to thieves.
I know the roads, the fords and the thieves on them. Whether that keeps your wagons safe or empties someone else's is up to you.
A guide of the Dwarf-road, cast out for selling caravan routes to Bree-land thieves. I still know every road in Eriador.
Telchar of Nogrod forged Narsil. No smith of Nogrod has matched him since, but some of us try...

I was a master of the forges of Nogrod, where Telchar once worked. I made blades for the Firebeard lords and mended heirlooms older than the halls they hung in. Mending was not enough. I read every scrap of Telchar's craft that survived, and I tried his quenching in the old dark forges under the city.

My apprentices worked those forges as hard as I did. One of them lost his hand when a quench cracked the crucible, and his clan went to the guild. The guild said I drove the young too hard and sought a craft that was not mine to seek. They broke my mark and barred me from every forge in the Blue Mountains.
The boy knew the danger and chose to stay. The guild wanted a reason, and I gave them one. I can still forge what no smith west of the Misty Mountains can, and I mean to finish what Telchar began.
A master's craft should not be chained by the guild's caution.
A boy lost his hand, and you still call it his choice.
I make steel others cannot. Keep me in iron and coal and you will not be sorry.
A master smith of Nogrod, barred from the forges after an apprentice was maimed chasing Telchar's lost craft.
The Broadbeams of Belegost stood against a dragon once. We have not forgotten how to stand...

I was raised in the old way of Belegost: hammer and shield, the slow advance, no step back. I served twenty years in the Broadbeam guard and kept the outer gates against goblins and worse. My fathers' fathers faced Glaurung in the masks of Belegost, and I meant to be worthy of them.

Our halls grow fat on trade now, and Elves from the Havens walk our market as if they owned it. One of them called our steel crude, so I broke his jaw. The lords paid the Havens for his teeth, and they paid me with dismissal.
Let the merchants bow to the Elves. The world still needs dwarves who know what a shield-wall is for, and orcs do not trade. My hammer goes where it can be of use.
Pride and a hard hand both have their place in a fight.
You broke a guest's jaw over a word about your steel.
I bring a hammer, a shield and a back that does not bend. That is enough.
A Broadbeam of the old school, dismissed for brawling with an Elf of the Havens. I want work for my hammer.
In the northern fells you see the goblin before it sees you, or you do not come home...

I was the youngest of seven brothers and the only one who could not swing a hammer worth the name, so I learned the crossbow and the art of keeping still. For years I led the scouts of Ironcrag, tracking the Blue Craig bands through the northern fells and bringing word back before they struck.

One spring a goblin chieftain asked to parley at the foot of the Craig, to buy back his captured sons. I went with the warden's envoy, and when the chieftain came down to meet us I put a bolt through his throat. The warden called it murder under a flag of truce and took my company from me.
That chieftain burned two of our steadings the year before, and I would shoot him again. But the warden wants scouts who keep their word to goblins, so I sell my eyes and my bolts elsewhere.
A goblin who burns steadings has no claim on anyone's word.
You broke a truce. What is your word worth now?
I see what moves in the hills before it reaches you, and I shoot straight. Keep your parleys to yourself.
A scout of Ironcrag who shot a goblin chieftain at a parley. Cast out, but still the best eyes in the fells.
My line has died with an axe in its hand for three generations. I do not expect to break the habit...

My grandfather fell at Azanulbizar under the gates of Moria, and my father in the wars against Blue Craig. I stood in the vanguard from the day I could lift a shield, and when raiders struck the Dwarf-road I led the company that hunted them down. We were never slow.

Last summer we caught a band of Men who had robbed our wagons near the borders of the Shire. They threw down their weapons and asked for the warden's judgement. I gave them mine instead, there on the road. Shire-folk saw it, the Thain sent word to Thorin's Halls, and the king could not keep me after that.
Robbers are robbers, and a judge's hall is a long way from the road. I will not pretend to be sorry. War is the only trade I know, and the world has plenty of it.
Robbers who leave the road alive rob again.
They surrendered, and you killed them. That is not war.
Three generations of my line died fighting. Point me at your enemy and I will do the same, or better.
A warrior of a fighting line, cast out for killing robbers who had surrendered. War is all I know.
Iron is iron, says the buyer, until he weighs it...

I ran the iron trade from Thorin's Halls to the Havens: bar iron down the Lune to the shipwrights of Harlond, tools and nails along the Dwarf-road to the Shire. I knew the prices in every market from Michel Delving to Mithlond, and I could keep a caravan fed and guarded on half what others spent.

The Elves pay well and check little, or so I thought. For two years my bars to Harlond carried a core of slag under good iron, until a shipwright of the Havens split one on his anvil. The Elves shut their quays to Thorin's Halls for a season, and the merchants' guild handed me to the king to open them again.

The guild cheats with its own weights, only more carefully. I fled before the hearing with what I could carry. I still know every price and every buyer in Eriador, and a captain who wants his stores bought cheap has a use for me.
Shrewd, if crooked. A good quartermaster is worth a little crookedness.
You sold the Elves slag and shamed your whole people.
I will keep your company fed, armed and paid for less than you think. Do not ask how.
An iron trader of Thorin's Halls who sold the Elves slag for iron. Exiled, but I can buy anything cheap.
A dwarf's word, once given, is harder than any stone in the Blue Mountains...

I commanded the garrison of Dolmed Hold, a company of the best axes in the Wardens' service. I earned that rank by holding my line and keeping my word, and my company would have followed me into a dragon's mouth. We kept the passes and the steadings in the hills below them.

When the Blue Craig host came south one winter, the lord of the Wardens ordered us back to guard the mine-heads. That left the hill steadings of Men to the goblins, folk I had sworn to defend. I marched to the steadings instead, and we held them. My lord said a captain who chooses his own orders cannot keep his command.
He was within his right, and I do not quarrel with it. But I gave my word to those Men and I kept it. I will serve a lord who wants a captain like that, if there is one.
You kept your oath when it cost you everything. That is rare.
A captain who disobeys once will disobey again.
I lead with honor and fight to win. Give me your trust and you will have mine.
A captain of Dolmed Hold who kept his oath to the hill-folk against his lord's orders. My word still holds.
The deeps of Nogrod have lain flooded since the First Age. I meant to drain them...

I built the engines of the Blue Mountains: the great pumps that clear the drowned galleries under Nogrod, the lifts at Hammerdeep and the wheeled arbalests the Firebeards haul up to the walls. I could make water climb a mountain and send a bolt through a door. The guild called me the best engineer of my age.

A miller from the Shire came to Thorin's Halls to ask how to keep his mill-race from flooding. I drew him a sluice and a pump and thought no more of it. When the guild heard I had given dwarf-craft to a hobbit for nothing, they struck my name from the engineers' rolls. Our crafts are not for outsiders, they said.
I do not regret it. The miller's family eats because of that sluice, and dwarf-craft lost nothing by it. But the guild is the guild, so I build for anyone with honest work for an engineer.
A craft shared freely does more good than one locked away.
Your guild's secrets kept your people strong, and you gave them away.
I build engines that pump, lift and shoot. Give me timber, iron and time, and I will build them for you.
An engineer of Nogrod, struck from the guild's rolls for sharing dwarf-craft with a hobbit. My work is for anyone honest.
The road from the Old Ford to the Carrock is longer than it looks, friend.

I rode the post between Beorn's Hall and the Old Ford, carrying letters, coin and now and then a sick child to the healer. Every rider on that road knew me, and I knew every ford and farm along the Great River.

One autumn the grain wagon I was guarding came upon a village burned out by orcs down from the High Pass. I gave the families half the load without asking leave. The steward called it theft and wrote my name in his tally.
No hall will hire a man marked for that, so I ride for whoever pays, and I still stop at every farm on the way. I cannot seem to help it. My horse is all that is left of that life.
Feeding the hungry is no crime to me.
A rider who gives away other men's grain is a poor courier.
Trust me with a message, a purse or a wounded man, and I will carry it anywhere you point.
Riders of the Vale roads know every ford between the Carrock and the Gladden Fields. We go wherever the roads still need carrying.
My name is older than my fortune. Have you heard of the House of Beorn?
My family claims kinship with the House of Beorn, so I was taught young to lead men and to sit a horse. I rose to command thirty spears on the Old Forest Road.

I held a ford on the Great River with thirty spears when a larger band of orcs came down from the mountains. My captain withdrew in the night and left us the order to hold. I held it, and eleven men died before help arrived.

The Folk of the Old Ford praised the stand and then quietly passed me over for every command, because I had named my captain's flight aloud. I carry the eleven names with me. A man who will not lie for his betters finds few doors open.
You did what honor asked of you.
Perhaps your captain saw the field better than you did.
If you need someone to hold a line and keep faith with the men in it, I will lead a company for you.
The sons of the old Vale houses are raised to lead men and to ride out when the horns sound. Some of us find our commands elsewhere.
Looking for someone who knows the roads. I do.
I scouted for the trading parties that run from the Old Ford to Gladden Hold and the High Pass. Water, ambush ground, safe fords, I priced them all. A good scout is paid by the mile.

When the orc raids went quiet, the party's master tried to cut my wage and said there was no danger left to pay for. Quiet was my work. I took my maps and left him to find his own way, and two carts were lost that season.
No trader trusts me now, and I trust none of them back. I carry my own pay and I count it twice.
A man should be paid for his craft.
You left honest drivers to the raiders.
Pay me on time and I will put you on the best ground between here and the Carrock.
Trade scouts of the Vales sell the roads they know to anyone who pays on time. We are not sentimental about it.
A man of the Old Ford, far from his river. Try not to laugh, I have heard it all.

I walked the landings of the Old Ford with the watch, a long spear in my hands, keeping thieves out of the ferry sheds. Hold a spear steady on a rocking ferry deck for ten years and you can use it anywhere.

I noticed the ford-wardens taking more silver in tolls than they ever wrote down. I kept my own tally and took it to the elders, and I was struck from the watch rolls before the ink dried. The week before, I had let a starving boy go, so I was blamed for that too.
So here I am, a watchman without a ford, holding a tally nobody wants. I keep it anyway, in case a better council ever asks.
Counting honestly should never cost a man his post.
A watchman who frees thieves has himself to blame.
I can hold a spear steady on any ground, and I can read your quartermaster's books, for a fair share.
I learned the long spear on the pitching decks of the Old Ford ferries. Few things steady the hand like that.
The lads call me Bear, after the old chieftain. I have not earned it yet, but I will.

My father told the tale of Beorn every night of my childhood. The other boys named me Bear as a joke because I would not stop asking for more of it. At sixteen I took a spear from the armory of Beorn's Hall and swore to make the joke true.
Word came of orcs near our hills, and I led six lads out to meet them without waiting for the garrison. I never counted the enemy, and there were forty. Three of the six came home.
The garrison does not trust me with a command now, and my father will not speak of it. I would sooner die useful than live as a joke. I still carry the spear.
Courage learns from its mistakes.
You threw boys at forty orcs for the sake of a nickname.
Let me stand in your front rank, and I will earn what the lads called me or learn I never could.
Young spearmen of the Vales grow up on the tales of Beorn. Some of us go looking for a fight that big.
Forgive me, I only wished to see a friendly face.

My father fished the Great River and I fished it after him, hauling nets at dawn and mending them at dusk. When the watch needed spears, I took up the boat-hook and a place in the line, being strong and no worse than most.
When a wolf-rider band crossed the shallows one winter night, I froze. The lads on either side of me did not. Two never came back, and I was crouched behind a drying rack when they fell.
I do not blame the cold, for I know what I did. Since then I give away what coin I earn to the widows of Eastbank, and it is never enough.
Fear touches every man. You have paid for it.
A man who breaks from the line is no use to me.
If you can use a man who knows his own failing, I will carry a spear for you and try to stand firmer than I did.
Fishermen of the Great River take up the boat-hook and the spear when the watch calls. Not all of us stand when the shouting starts.
You carry a bow? Good. Then you will understand.

I was the best archer in the Vales at twenty, with a black-fletched arrow on my quiver in honor of the Wardens of the Carrock. The great shoot at the midsummer fair at Honeymead was mine to lose, and I wanted it badly.

A rival from Gladden Hold shot as well as I did, so the night before the final I cut his string a third of the way through. He drew at the line and it snapped across his cheek. They found the cut ends in my pack.

I was stripped of my fletching and barred from the butts. I still shoot better than any man in the hall, and they know it, and it changes nothing. I am not sorry I wanted to win, only that I was caught.
Skill like yours should not rot unused.
A man who cuts his rival's string deserves the ban.
Take me on and I will put an arrow wherever you point. Do not ask me for more than that.
Archers of the Vales are raised on the Wardens' legend and shoot at the butts every feast day. Some of us carry the bow wherever the pay is fair.
Nothing watches a road like an old rider with a good horse.

My father was a boy when Beorn's Hall was raised, timber by timber, and I grew up watching the Vales fill with farms. I rode the High Pass post for twenty years, carrying word between the old watch above the pass and the hall.

One spring the watchmen saw a goblin muster gathering in the mountains, and I rode to the council with it. The elder called watch-tales gossip and kept me waiting three weeks. By the time he believed it, the villages under the pass had burned.
I kept my honor and lost my post, since the elder could not forgive having been wrong. Now I ride where a warning is still welcome. It is a short list.
You were right, and they should have listened.
Watch-tales bring rumor. A sensible elder waits for proof.
I know the mountain roads and the minds of men who ignore warnings. I will ride ahead for you.
I come from the riders of the High Pass Watch, who watch the mountain roads for the Vales. A warning from us is sound, whatever the elders choose to do with it.
Hard country makes hard men. Do not expect me to apologize.

I served as a sergeant on the High Pass road, where the spearmen of the Vales stand beside the Wardens of the Carrock against whatever comes down from the mountains. The Wardens taught me to keep the spear steady and the line closed, and to waste nothing, pity included.

We took a band of goblin raiders who had burned three farms, and I put the prisoners down rather than march them for days to the stocks. My captain called it murder. The Wardens said nothing, which I took for agreement.
I was dismissed with no pay owed and no word to carry. I would do it again. The farms along that road stayed safe the rest of the year.
Hard choices keep the roads safe.
Killing prisoners is plain murder.
I fight hard and I do not flinch. If that suits you, put me at the front of your line.
The spearmen of the Vales hold the High Pass road beside the Wardens, and the work there is not gentle. We learn it, and we do not forget it.
Have you heard whether the Carrock meadows are quiet this season?
I bred and broke horses on the meadows below the Carrock, where the grass is sweet and the horses are hardy. I rode before I could properly walk, and half the mounts in the valley carry my training.

Orcs came down at harvest and drove off our herd and half our village. I rode to Beorn's Hall for help, but the council would not hear me before morning, so I gathered the farmhands and went after them myself.

We took back most of the horses and every child, but two farmhands did not return, and the village is a burned ring of posts. I sold the herd to pay the dead men's families. A rider's hands are all I have left.
You gave everything you had. That counts.
A hothead who rides off without leave gets men killed.
I will ride for you gladly, and I will give my last coin to anyone you want to help.
Horse-breeders of the Carrock meadows raise sturdy mounts and riders who ask little. We are quick to the saddle when the raiders come.
The Old Forest Road from Woodmen-town to the Forest Gate is longer than it looks, friend.

I rode the post between Woodmen-town and the Forest Gate, carrying letters, coin and now and then a sick child to the healer. Every rider on that road knew me, and I knew every glade and farm along the eaves of Mirkwood.

One autumn the grain wagon I was guarding came upon Hazelglade, burned out by orcs out of the shadow of Dol Guldur. I gave the families half the load without asking leave. The reeve called it theft and wrote my name in his ledger.
No hall will hire a man marked for that, so I ride for whoever pays, and I still stop at every farm on the way. I cannot seem to help it. My horse is all that is left of that life.
Feeding the hungry is no crime to me.
A rider who gives away other men's grain is a poor courier.
Trust me with a message, a purse or a wounded man, and I will carry it anywhere you point.
Riders of the Forest Road know every glade between the Forest Gate and Ironwood Hall. We go wherever the roads still need carrying.
My name is older than my fortune. Have you heard of the House of Angáladh?
My family claims kinship with the House of Angáladh and the old kings of the Woodmen, so I was taught young to lead men and to sit a horse. I rose to command thirty spears on the Old Forest Road.

I held a ford near Thornbrook with thirty spears when a larger band of orcs came through from the south. My captain withdrew in the night and left us the order to hold. I held it, and eleven men died before help arrived.

The council praised the ford and then quietly passed me over for every command, because I had named my captain's flight aloud. I carry the eleven names with me. A man who will not lie for his betters finds few doors open.
You did what honor asked of you.
Perhaps your captain saw the field better than you did.
If you need someone to hold a line and keep faith with the men in it, I will lead a company for you.
The sons of the old Woodmen houses are raised to lead men and to ride out when the horns sound. Some of us find our commands elsewhere.
Looking for someone who knows the roads. I do.

I scouted for the trading parties that run from Woodmen-town to Ironwood Hall and the borders of the Woodland Realm. Water, ambush ground, safe glades, I priced them all. A good scout is paid by the mile.

When the spiders went quiet on the road, the party's master tried to cut my wage and said there was no danger left to pay for. Quiet was my work. I took my maps and left him to find his own way, and two carts were lost that season.
No trader trusts me now, and I trust none of them back. I carry my own pay and I count it twice.
A man should be paid for his craft.
You left honest drivers to the spiders.
Pay me on time and I will put you on the best ground between here and Emyn Duir.
Trade scouts of the Woodmen sell the paths they know to anyone who pays on time. We are not sentimental about it.
A Woodman out of the forest, and no use in the open. Try not to laugh, I have heard it all.

I walked the plank-ways of Woodmen-town with the watch, a long spear in my hands, keeping thieves out of the market stalls. Hold a spear steady on a swaying walkway between the great oaks for ten years and you can use it anywhere.

I noticed the toll-men at the Forest Gate taking more silver than they ever wrote down. I kept my own tally and took it to the council, and I was struck from the watch rolls before the ink dried. The week before, I had let a starving boy go, so I was blamed for that too.
So here I am, a watchman without a town, holding a ledger nobody wants. I keep the tally anyway, in case a better council ever asks.
Counting honestly should never cost a man his post.
A watchman who frees thieves has himself to blame.
I can hold a spear steady on any ground, and I can read your quartermaster's books, for a fair share.
I learned the long spear on the swaying plank-ways of Woodmen-town. Few things steady the hand like that.
The lads call me Spiderbane. I have not earned it yet, but I will.

My father told the tale of the great spider of Emyn Duir every night of my childhood. The other boys named me Spiderbane as a joke because I would not stop asking for more of it. At sixteen I took a spear from the armory at Thornhold and swore to make the joke true.
Word came of orcs near our clearings, and I led six lads out to meet them without waiting for the garrison. I never counted the enemy, and there were forty. Three of the six came home.
The garrison does not trust me with a command now, and my father will not speak of it. I would sooner die useful than live as a joke. I still carry the spear.
Courage learns from its mistakes.
You threw boys at forty orcs for the sake of a nickname.
Let me stand in your front rank, and I will earn what the lads called me or learn I never could.
Young spearmen of the Woodmen grow up on the tales of the spiders of Emyn Duir. Some of us go looking for a fight that big.
Forgive me, I only wished to see a friendly face.

My father felled timber at Fellingwick and I felled it after him, swinging the axe at dawn and sharpening it at dusk. When the watch needed spears, I took up a boar-spear and a place in the line, being strong and no worse than most.
When a raiding band came out of the trees one winter night, I froze. The lads on either side of me did not. Two never came back, and I was crouched behind a woodpile when they fell.
I do not blame the cold, for I know what I did. Since then I give away what coin I earn to the widows of Fellingwick, and it is never enough.
Fear touches every man. You have paid for it.
A man who breaks from the line is no use to me.
If you can use a man who knows his own failing, I will carry a spear for you and try to stand firmer than I did.
Woodcutters of Mirkwood's eaves take up the boar-spear when the watch calls. Not all of us stand when the shouting starts.
You carry a bow? Good. Then you will understand.

I was the best archer among the Woodmen at twenty, with a black-fletched arrow on my quiver in honor of the Woodwards of the Forest Road. The great shoot at the midsummer fair in Woodmen-town was mine to lose, and I wanted it badly.

A rival from Ironwood Hall shot as well as I did, so the night before the final I cut his string a third of the way through. He drew at the line and it snapped across his cheek. They found the cut ends in my pack.

I was stripped of my fletching and barred from the butts. I still shoot better than any man in the hall, and they know it, and it changes nothing. I am not sorry I wanted to win, only that I was caught.
Skill like yours should not rot unused.
A man who cuts his rival's string deserves the ban.
Take me on and I will put an arrow wherever you point. Do not ask me for more than that.
Archers of the Woodmen are raised on the Woodwards' legend and shoot at the butts every feast day. Some of us carry the bow wherever the pay is fair.
Nothing watches a road like an old rider with a good horse.

My father was a boy when Woodmen-town was palisaded, and I grew up watching the clearings creep back into the forest's edge. I rode the Emyn Duir Watch post for twenty years, carrying word between the old watch above the trees and the gates.

One spring the watch-smoke rose from Emyn Duir with news of an orc muster to the south, and I rode to the council with it. The lord called smoke-talk gossip and kept me waiting three weeks. By the time he believed it, the villages on the eaves had burned.
I kept my honor and lost my post, since the lord could not forgive having been wrong. Now I ride where a warning is still welcome. It is a short list.
You were right, and they should have listened.
Smoke brings rumor. A sensible lord waits for proof.
I know the southern roads and the minds of men who ignore warnings. I will ride ahead for you.
I come from the Emyn Duir Watch riders, who watch the southern roads for the Woodmen. A warning from us is sound, whatever the lords choose to do with it.
Hard country makes hard men. Do not expect me to apologize.

I served as a sergeant on the Emyn Duir road, where the spearmen of the Woodmen stand beside the Wardens of Emyn Duir against whatever comes up from Dol Guldur. The Wardens taught me to keep the spear steady and the line closed, and to waste nothing, pity included.

We took a band of raiders in the pay of Dol Guldur who had burned three farms, and I put the prisoners down rather than march them for days to the stocks. My captain called it murder. The Wardens said nothing, which I took for agreement.
I was dismissed with no pay owed and no word to carry. I would do it again. The farms along that road stayed safe the rest of the year.
Hard choices keep the roads safe.
Killing prisoners is plain murder.
I fight hard and I do not flinch. If that suits you, put me at the front of your line.
The spearmen of the Woodmen hold the Emyn Duir road beside the Wardens, and the work there is not gentle. We learn it, and we do not forget it.
Have you heard whether the southern glades are quiet this season?

I bred and broke horses in the clearings below Emyn Duir, where the grass is thin between the trees and the horses are hardy. I rode before I could properly walk, and half the mounts in the eaves carry my training.

Raiders out of the south came at harvest and drove off our herd and half our village. I rode to Woodmen-town for help, but the council would not hear me before morning, so I gathered the farmhands and went after them myself.

We took back most of the horses and every child, but two farmhands did not return, and the village is a burned ring of posts. I sold the herd to pay the dead men's families. A rider's hands are all I have left.
You gave everything you had. That counts.
A hothead who rides off without leave gets men killed.
I will ride for you gladly, and I will give my last coin to anyone you want to help.
Horse-breeders of the Emyn Duir clearings raise sturdy mounts and riders who ask little. We are quick to the saddle when the raiders come.
The road from Vineholm to Redwater is longer than it looks, friend.

I rode the post between Vineholm and Redwater, carrying letters, coin and now and then a sick child to the healer. Every rider on that road knew me, and I knew every ford and farm along the River Running.

One autumn the grain wagon I was guarding came upon a village burned out by raiders from Rhûn. I gave the families half the load without asking leave. The wine factor called it theft and wrote my name in his ledger.
No vintner will hire a man marked for that, so I ride for whoever pays, and I still stop at every farm on the way. I cannot seem to help it. My horse is all that is left of that life.
Feeding the hungry is no crime to me.
A rider who gives away other men's grain is a poor courier.
Trust me with a message, a purse or a wounded man, and I will carry it anywhere you point.
Riders of the Dorwinion roads know every landing between Vineholm and the Sea of Rhûn. We go wherever the roads still need carrying.
My name is older than my fortune. Have you heard of the House of Vineholm?

My family claims kinship with the House of Vineholm, who planted the first terraces above the river, so I was taught young to lead men and to sit a horse. I rose to command thirty spears on the eastern road.

I held a ford on the Redwater with thirty spears when a larger band came through from the east. My captain withdrew in the night and left us the order to hold. I held it, and eleven men died before help arrived.

The council praised the ford and then quietly passed me over for every command, because I had named my captain's flight aloud. I carry the eleven names with me. A man who will not lie for his betters finds few doors open.
You did what honor asked of you.
Perhaps your captain saw the field better than you did.
If you need someone to hold a line and keep faith with the men in it, I will lead a company for you.
The sons of Dorwinion's old vintner houses are raised to lead men and to ride out when the horns sound. Some of us find our commands elsewhere.
Looking for someone who knows the roads. I do.
I scouted for the wine caravans that run from Vineholm to the Sea of Rhûn landings and the Northgate road. Water, ambush ground, safe fords, I priced them all. A good scout is paid by the mile.

When the Easterling raids went quiet, the caravan master tried to cut my wage and said there was no danger left to pay for. Quiet was my work. I took my maps and left him to find his own way, and two carts were lost that season.
No factor trusts me now, and I trust none of them back. I carry my own pay and I count it twice.
A man should be paid for his craft.
You left honest drivers to the raiders.
Pay me on time and I will put you on the best ground between here and the sea.
Caravan scouts of Dorwinion sell the roads they know to anyone who pays on time. We are not sentimental about it.
A man of Redwater on dry land. Try not to laugh, I have heard it all.

I walked the quays of Redwater Landing with the town watch, a boat-spear in my hands, keeping thieves out of the cask yards. Hold a long spear on a rocking deck for ten years and you can use it anywhere.

I noticed the harbor-master's toll-men taking more silver than they ever wrote down. I kept my own tally and took it to the council, and I was struck from the watch rolls before the ink dried. The week before, I had let a starving boy go, so I was blamed for that too.
So here I am, a watchman without a harbor, holding a ledger nobody wants. I keep the tally anyway, in case a better council ever asks.
Counting honestly should never cost a man his post.
A watchman who frees thieves has himself to blame.
I can hold a spear steady on any ground, and I can read your quartermaster's books, for a fair share.
I learned the long spear on the pitching decks of the Redwater watch. Few things steady the hand like that.
The lads named me after Ostmar the Warden. I have not earned it yet, but I will.

My father told the tale of Ostmar, who held Northgate through a whole winter, every night of my childhood. The other boys named me after the Warden as a joke because I would not stop asking for more of it. At sixteen I took a spear from the Vineholm armory and swore to make the joke true.
Word came of raiders from Rhûn near our hills, and I led six lads out to meet them without waiting for the garrison. I never counted the enemy, and there were forty. Three of the six came home.
The garrison does not trust me with a command now, and my father will not speak of it. I would sooner die useful than live as a joke. I still carry the spear.
Courage learns from its mistakes.
You threw boys at forty men for the sake of a nickname.
Let me stand in your front rank, and I will earn what the lads called me or learn I never could.
Young spearmen of Dorwinion grow up on the tale of Ostmar the Warden. Some of us go looking for a fight that big.
Forgive me, I only wished to see a friendly face.

My father fished the Sea of Rhûn and I fished it after him, hauling nets at dawn and mending them at dusk. When the watch needed spears, I took up the boat-hook and a place in the line, being strong and no worse than most.
When a raiding band came up out of the reeds in a morning fog, I froze. The lads on either side of me did not. Two never came back, and I was crouched behind a net-rack when they fell.
I do not blame the fog, for I know what I did. Since then I give away what coin I earn to the widows of Seagate, and it is never enough.
