Fear touches every man. You have paid for it.
A man who breaks from the line is no use to me.
If you can use a man who knows his own failing, I will carry a spear for you and try to stand firmer than I did.
Fishermen of the Sea of Rhûn take up the boat-hook and the spear when the watch calls. Not all of us stand when the shouting starts.
You carry a bow? Good. Then you will understand.
I was the best archer in Dorwinion at twenty, with a white-fletched arrow on my quiver in honor of the Vineholm butts. The great shoot at the vintage fair was mine to lose, and I wanted it badly.

A rival from Seagate shot as well as I did, so the night before the final I cut his string a third of the way through. He drew at the line and it snapped across his cheek. They found the cut ends in my pack.

I was stripped of my fletching and barred from the butts. I still shoot better than any man in the hall, and they know it, and it changes nothing. I am not sorry I wanted to win, only that I was caught.
Skill like yours should not rot unused.
A man who cuts his rival's string deserves the ban.
Take me on and I will put an arrow wherever you point. Do not ask me for more than that.
Archers of Dorwinion shoot at the butts every vintage feast. Some of us carry the bow wherever the pay is fair.
Nothing watches a road like an old rider with a good horse.

My grandmother planted the first vines on the Amberslope terraces, and I grew up watching Dorwinion's presses and cellars rise year by year. I rode the Northgate post for twenty years, carrying word between the beacon tower above the keep and the gates of Vineholm.

One spring the beacon-keepers sent word of an Easterling muster in the east, and I rode to the council with it. The lord called beacon-smoke gossip and kept me waiting three weeks. By the time he believed it, the villages on the eastern slopes had burned.
I kept my honor and lost my post, since the lord could not forgive having been wrong. Now I ride where a warning is still welcome. It is a short list.
You were right, and they should have listened.
Beacon-keepers see smoke and call it fire. A sensible lord waits for proof.
I know the eastern roads and the minds of men who ignore warnings. I will ride ahead for you.
I come from the Northgate riders, who watch the eastern roads for Dorwinion. A warning from us is sound, whatever the lords choose to do with it.
Hard country makes hard men. Do not expect me to apologize.

I served as a sergeant on the Eastmarch road, where Dorwinion's spearmen stand against whatever comes out of Rhûn. The old wardens taught me to keep the spear steady and the line closed, and to waste nothing, pity included.

We took a band of Easterling raiders who had burned three vineyards, and I put the prisoners down rather than march them for days to the stocks. My captain called it murder. The old wardens said nothing, which I took for agreement.
I was dismissed with no pay owed and no word to carry. I would do it again. The farms along that road stayed safe the rest of the year.
Hard choices keep the roads safe.
Killing prisoners is plain murder.
I fight hard and I do not flinch. If that suits you, put me at the front of your line.
Dorwinion's spearmen hold the Eastmarch road against all comers, and the work there is not gentle. We learn it, and we do not forget it.
Have you heard whether the eastern slopes are quiet this season?
I bred and broke horses on the downs east of the Redwater, where the grass is thin and the horses are hardy. I rode before I could properly walk, and half the mounts in the valley carry my training.

Raiders from Rhûn came at harvest and drove off our herd and half our village. I rode to Vineholm for help, but the council would not hear me before morning, so I gathered the farmhands and went after them myself.

We took back most of the horses and every child, but two farmhands did not return, and the village is a burned ring of posts. I sold the herd to pay the dead men's families. A rider's hands are all I have left.
You gave everything you had. That counts.
A hothead who rides off without leave gets men killed.
I will ride for you gladly, and I will give my last coin to anyone you want to help.
Horse-breeders of the eastern downs raise sturdy mounts and riders who ask little. We are quick to the saddle when the raiders come.
The horses grow restless, and strange wolves prowl the southern eaves...

I was a Marshal of Westmark, commanding a riding company of thirty. We patrolled from Westmark to the Southwood, watching the edge of Mirkwood for threats from Dol Guldur and beyond. But dark rumors came out of the forest.

My scouts reported strange activity: fires burning in the trees night after night, hunters who never came back, and wolves unlike any we had seen. When I brought word to Vidugard, the King's steward Aldwulf dismissed my concerns and said the hill was empty and the tales were for children.

I pressed the matter, and was relieved of command for 'spreading panic.' Now I ride alone, gathering proof of the threat. The King grows deaf under his steward's counsel while danger gathers at our doorstep.
A watchful eye may save the plains yet.
Perhaps you see threats where none exist.
I offer my lance and knowledge of these lands, if you need them.
Marshals of Westmark ride the long line between the plains and the forest eaves, and we trust our own eyes before any steward's word.
The blood of the old kings of Vidugard runs hot in my veins, demanding action...
I rode with the cavalry of Wainwatch, defending the eastern plains from Wainrider raids. My spear drank deep of enemy blood, and my horse Dustmane was known across Rhovanion for his speed.

During a skirmish, we pursued a raiding band too far and discovered they wore mail stamped by the envoy from Rhun, who feasted at our King's table as a friend. When I reported this to my captain, he ordered me to forget what I had seen. He said the King's steward had forbidden such talk.
I could not stay silent while treachery festered. I left my company and now ride as a masterless warrior, seeking those who still have the courage to face hard truths.
The plains need warriors who won't be silenced.
Disobedience weakens the realm.
My spear and steed are yours, if you'll have them.
The riders of Wainwatch hold the eastern plains against every raid, and we carry the old kings' pride into every charge. Some of us ride on alone.
Young blood seeks glory, but finds only shadow...

I earned my first horse at twelve, my first kill at sixteen. I rode with the younger riders of Vidugard, eager to prove ourselves worthy of our fathers' legacies. We dreamed of great charges and heroic songs.

On patrol near the Southwood eaves, we found burnt villages, not raided by Wainriders, but destroyed by men on foot. The tracks led toward Dol Guldur. When we reported this, we were told we were mistaken, that Wainrider raiders were to blame.

But I know horse tracks from wolf tracks, boot prints from orc spoor. Someone wanted those villages gone, and it wasn't the Wainriders. I left my company to seek the truth. The plains are threatened from within and without.
Youth often sees clearly what age ignores.
Young eyes can mistake shadows for substance.
I offer eager strength and sharp eyes, if you'll have them.
Young riders of Vidugard are raised on tales of great charges. Some of us learn early that the real enemy leaves no banner.
Honor lost is harder to bear than any wound...

I was thane of a small hall near Westmark, sworn to the Riders of Southwood. My people looked to me for protection and justice. I had good riders, strong walls, and fertile meadows. It should have been enough.

The steward Aldwulf came with tax collectors, demanding twice our usual tribute. When I protested, he accused me of hoarding wealth while the King's treasury ran thin. He had documents, forged but convincing, showing I'd traded with the Wainriders.

The King, trusting his steward, stripped me of lands and title. My own people were told I was a traitor. Now I wander, a thane without a hall, seeking to restore my name through deeds since words failed me.
Aldwulf has destroyed many good men.
Perhaps there was cause for suspicion.
I offer a warrior's skill and bitter experience, if you'll take them.
Thanes of the plains hold small halls and large pride. When a hall falls, its lord rides on with nothing but his name.
The shield-maidens of old knew no fear, neither should I...

My grandmother rode with the host in her youth, before marriage tamed her. She taught me spear and horse in secret, despite my father's wishes. When raiders struck our village while the men were away, I led the defense.

We held, but I was seen fighting. The village elders said I brought shame, that women who took up arms invited chaos. They demanded I marry immediately or leave. My father, fearing scandal, sided with them.
I chose exile over chains. Now I ride as my grandmother once did, free and fierce. The plains need every spear, regardless of who wields it. Let them whisper, I'll be too busy fighting to hear.
The realm wastes half its strength ignoring women warriors.
Tradition exists for good reasons.
I offer a shield-maiden's courage, if you'll accept it.
Some daughters of the plains ride and fight as their grandmothers did. The villages call it shame, and the raiders call it a mistake.
The weak die so the strong might live, such is war...

I rode with the most aggressive company of Wainwatch. We gave no quarter to the Wainriders, pursuing them to extinction. My commander said mercy to enemies was cruelty to our own people. I believed him.

We caught a band of raiders stealing horses. My captain ordered them all killed, men, women, children. I obeyed, but one boy reminded me of my own son. After that night, I couldn't stop seeing his face.
I left before I lost what humanity remained. Now I fight only those who can fight back. The line between warrior and butcher is thinner than most admit. I've been both, and prefer the former.
Recognition of evil is the first step to redemption.
War demands terrible choices.
I offer hard skills and harder lessons, if you need them.
The riders of the Wainwatch frontier learn war without mercy. Not all of us can live with what we learn.
The bow sings truest from horseback...

My father bred horses, my mother was from the Southwood, where archery is prized. I combined both traditions, becoming one of the few horse archers in the realm. I could put an arrow through a ring at full gallop.

Scouting near Dol Guldur, I saw things that shouldn't exist: pits, strange fires, and twisted creatures. When I tried to get closer, wolves pursued me, but wolves that ran upright and spoke in dark tongues.
My captain didn't believe me, said I'd been drinking. The steward heard my tale and declared me mad, suggesting I be confined. I fled that night. What I saw was real, and the plains must be warned.
Dark times bring forth dark creatures.
Fear can make men see monsters.
My bow and knowledge are yours, if you'll trust them.
Horse archers of the Southwood shoot as well from the saddle as from the ground. We see farther than the halls care to know.
The horses whisper of storms approaching...
I was born in the saddle, or near enough. My family supplied horses to the King's own stables at Vidugard. I could ride before I could properly walk, and understood horses better than people.

The horses began refusing to go near the road toward Dol Guldur, and even the bravest stallions would rear and flee. Animals sense evil before men do. When I reported this to the horse masters, they blamed bad training.

But I know horses. They weren't spooked, they were terrified. Something unnatural grows beneath the forest's southern shadow. I left the royal stables to investigate on my own. If the horses fear it, we should too.
Animals often sense what men miss.
Horses spook at many things.
I offer a rider's skill and a horse's wisdom, if you'll have them.
Horse-masters of Vidugard trust the herd before the hall. A frightened stallion has saved more riders than any scout.
The finest riders serve truth, not corrupted counsel...

I was chosen for the King's own guard, the elite who ride beside the Horse-lord. It was the highest honor a rider could achieve. I served with pride, until I saw how far the King's court had fallen under his steward's influence.

The King, once mighty, now sits grey and weary while Aldwulf whispers poison. I heard orders given that made no sense: troops withdrawn from threatened borders, supplies sent to uncertain destinations.
When I questioned these orders, Aldwulf marked me as 'unreliable.' I was reassigned to distant patrols, then dismissed entirely. I won't serve a puppet court while the real threats gather strength.
Loyalty to the realm surpasses loyalty to its ruler.
Abandoning your king seems like treachery.
I offer elite training and unwavering purpose, if you need them.
The King's guard of Vidugard rides at his side in every hall and on every field. When the court rots, some of us ride away.
The plains taught me more than any hall of warriors ever could...

I grew up on the meadows near Wainwatch, where the wild horses still run free and the Wainriders probe our borders. My father was a herder, not a soldier, but he taught me to read the land and the wind.
When raiders came, our village had no riding company to protect it. I rallied the young riders and we drove them off ourselves. Word spread, and the Marshal offered me a place in the muster.

But the marshals quarrel among themselves while the real enemy gathers. I left the muster to find a leader worth following, someone who sees beyond petty border disputes to the true darkness rising beneath Mirkwood.
A rider who knows the land is worth ten who only know the charge.
Leaving your people undefended seems reckless.
I know every trail and ford in Rhovanion, and my horse has never failed me. That is what I bring.
Herders' sons of the Wainwatch meadows learn the land before they learn the lance. We ride well, and we ride where we are needed.
